The **2010 Central Canada earthquake** occurred with a moment magnitude of 5.0 in Central Canada on 23 June at about 13:41:41 EDT and lasted about 30 seconds.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-GlobeAndMail-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-thestar.com-4) The epicentre was situated approximately 56 kilometres (35 mi) north of Ottawa, Ontario,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS-5) in the municipality of Val-des-Bois, Quebec.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Earthquake_hits-6) Canada's capital, Ottawa, declared this earthquake as being its most powerful in 65 years.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Ottawa_Citizen-7)

It was felt across most of Ontario[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-8) and Quebec, as well as parts of the northeastern United States,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Michigan-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Pittsburgh-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-12) in addition to places as far as Chicago,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-13)Pittsburgh,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-14)Baltimore, Charleston, West Virginia, and Halifax. It was the first moderate earthquake associated with the Western Quebec Seismic Zone since 20 April 2002, when the area was affected by magnitude 5.1 M w tremors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-17) Southern Ontario was also affected by the 1998 magnitude 5.2 M wPymatuning earthquake, associated with a different seismic region (Southern Great Lakes seismic zone).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-19)

Although a 5.0 magnitude quake is considered to be moderate, the earthquake's depth (estimates of which vary between 16.4 kilometres (10.2 mi) and 19.0 kilometres (11.8 mi))[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Earthquake_of_5.0_magnitude_hits_Ontario,_Quebec-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Geologists-21) meant that its effects were more widely felt.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-The_Great_Canada-22)

The magnitude 5.0 M wintraplate earthquake occurred near the southern edge of the Western Quebec Seismic Zone, known for frequent, but minor tremors, occurring, on average, every five days.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-23) Far away from the North Americantectonic plate's margin, the regional seismicity is controlled by a series of geologic faults formed over the last billion years by the processes of mountain building, including the Grenville orogeny, and subsequent erosion. The processes causing the earthquakes in the zone are not well understood: the tremors are not linked to particular seismogenic structures, nor are the sources of stress definitively identified.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-25) The initial focal mechanism of the 2010 earthquake suggests reverse faulting on a fault trending southeast–northwest. However, the size and depth of this earthquake make it uncertain whether the causative fault can be identified.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-26)
Earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 or greater are fairly infrequent in the area, occurring at a rate of a few per decade. Some studies suggest, however, that larger earthquakes of magnitude around 7 may have occurred 4550 and 7060 years BP.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-27)
USGS ShakeMap for the event

On 16 March 2011, a magnitude 3.7[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-37) or possibly 4.3[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-38) aftershock struck Hawkesbury, Ontario, on the Ottawa River Valley and southwest of the initial magnitude 5.0 epicentre. It was felt in places including Ottawa, Montreal and St. Albans, VT.

texts.1: The **2010 Central Canada earthquake** occurred with a moment magnitude of 5.0 in Central Canada on 23 June at about 13:41:41 EDT and lasted about 30 seconds.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-GlobeAndMail-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-thestar.com-4) The epicentre was situated approximately 56 kilometres (35 mi) north of Ottawa, Ontario,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS-5) in the municipality of Val-des-Bois, Quebec.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Earthquake_hits-6) Canada's capital, Ottawa, declared this earthquake as being its most powerful in 65 years.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Ottawa_Citizen-7)
texts.2: It was felt across most of Ontario[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-8) and Quebec, as well as parts of the northeastern United States,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Michigan-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Pittsburgh-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-12) in addition to places as far as Chicago,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-13)Pittsburgh,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-14)Baltimore, Charleston, West Virginia, and Halifax. It was the first moderate earthquake associated with the Western Quebec Seismic Zone since 20 April 2002, when the area was affected by magnitude 5.1 M w tremors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-17) Southern Ontario was also affected by the 1998 magnitude 5.2 M wPymatuning earthquake, associated with a different seismic region (Southern Great Lakes seismic zone).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-19)
texts.3: Although a 5.0 magnitude quake is considered to be moderate, the earthquake's depth (estimates of which vary between 16.4 kilometres (10.2 mi) and 19.0 kilometres (11.8 mi))[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Earthquake_of_5.0_magnitude_hits_Ontario,_Quebec-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Geologists-21) meant that its effects were more widely felt.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-The_Great_Canada-22)
texts.4:
The magnitude 5.0 M wintraplate earthquake occurred near the southern edge of the Western Quebec Seismic Zone, known for frequent, but minor tremors, occurring, on average, every five days.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-23) Far away from the North Americantectonic plate's margin, the regional seismicity is controlled by a series of geologic faults formed over the last billion years by the processes of mountain building, including the Grenville orogeny, and subsequent erosion. The processes causing the earthquakes in the zone are not well understood: the tremors are not linked to particular seismogenic structures, nor are the sources of stress definitively identified.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-25) The initial focal mechanism of the 2010 earthquake suggests reverse faulting on a fault trending southeast–northwest. However, the size and depth of this earthquake make it uncertain whether the causative fault can be identified.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-26)
Earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 or greater are fairly infrequent in the area, occurring at a rate of a few per decade. Some studies suggest, however, that larger earthquakes of magnitude around 7 may have occurred 4550 and 7060 years BP.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-27)
USGS ShakeMap for the event
texts.8:
On 16 March 2011, a magnitude 3.7[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-37) or possibly 4.3[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-38) aftershock struck Hawkesbury, Ontario, on the Ottawa River Valley and southwest of the initial magnitude 5.0 epicentre. It was felt in places including Ottawa, Montreal and St. Albans, VT.

The **2010 Central Canada earthquake** occurred with a moment magnitude of 5.0 in Central Canada on 23 June at about 13:41:41 EDT and lasted about 30 seconds.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-GlobeAndMail-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-thestar.com-4) The epicentre was situated approximately 56 kilometres (35 mi) north of Ottawa, Ontario,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS-5) in the municipality of Val-des-Bois, Quebec.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Earthquake_hits-6) Canada's capital, Ottawa, declared this earthquake as being its most powerful in 65 years.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Ottawa_Citizen-7)

It was felt across most of Ontario[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-8) and Quebec, as well as parts of the northeastern United States,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Michigan-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Pittsburgh-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-12) in addition to places as far as Chicago,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-13)Pittsburgh,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-14)Baltimore, Charleston, West Virginia, and Halifax. It was the first moderate earthquake associated with the Western Quebec Seismic Zone since 20 April 2002, when the area was affected by magnitude 5.1 M w tremors.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-17) Southern Ontario was also affected by the 1998 magnitude 5.2 M wPymatuning earthquake, associated with a different seismic region (Southern Great Lakes seismic zone).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-19)

Although a 5.0 magnitude quake is considered to be moderate, the earthquake's depth (estimates of which vary between 16.4 kilometres (10.2 mi) and 19.0 kilometres (11.8 mi))[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Earthquake_of_5.0_magnitude_hits_Ontario,_Quebec-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-Geologists-21) meant that its effects were more widely felt.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-The_Great_Canada-22)

The magnitude 5.0 M wintraplate earthquake occurred near the southern edge of the Western Quebec Seismic Zone, known for frequent, but minor tremors, occurring, on average, every five days.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-USGS_%E2%80%93_summary-15)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-23) Far away from the North Americantectonic plate's margin, the regional seismicity is controlled by a series of geologic faults formed over the last billion years by the processes of mountain building, including the Grenville orogeny, and subsequent erosion. The processes causing the earthquakes in the zone are not well understood: the tremors are not linked to particular seismogenic structures, nor are the sources of stress definitively identified.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-25) The initial focal mechanism of the 2010 earthquake suggests reverse faulting on a fault trending southeast–northwest. However, the size and depth of this earthquake make it uncertain whether the causative fault can be identified.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-26)
Earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 or greater are fairly infrequent in the area, occurring at a rate of a few per decade. Some studies suggest, however, that larger earthquakes of magnitude around 7 may have occurred 4550 and 7060 years BP.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-27)
USGS ShakeMap for the event

On 16 March 2011, a magnitude 3.7[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-37) or possibly 4.3[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Central_Canada_earthquake#cite_note-38) aftershock struck Hawkesbury, Ontario, on the Ottawa River Valley and southwest of the initial magnitude 5.0 epicentre. It was felt in places including Ottawa, Montreal and St. Albans, VT.

opened.anchor: Earthquakes in Canada: search 100,000 events since 1985
opened.information:
Source: https://canquery.com/blog/canada-earthquakes
Title: Earthquakes in Canada: search 100,000 events since 1985
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
Search, sort and chart Earthquakes Canada's record of 101,365 events from 1985 to 2019 by date, magnitude and province, and find recent events.
By CanQuery · Published October 25, 2026
Article updated October 25, 2026
Data links checked October 25, 2026
You want to know how often the ground shakes near you, find the largest earthquakes recorded in a province, or count events by year. Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) publishes the earthquakes located by Earthquakes Canada as open data. Its CSV file is a live table on CanQuery, so you can search, sort, filter and chart more than 100,000 events in the browser.
| At a glance |  |  
| --- | --- |  
| Publisher | Natural Resources Canada (Earthquakes Canada) |  
| What it lists | One row per located earthquake: time, position, depth, magnitude and nearest place |  
| Time span of the CSV | January 1, 1985 to December 31, 2019: 101,365 events |  
| Area | Canada and nearby areas, including parts of Alaska and Washington State |  
| On CanQuery | A live table in English and in French, with search, filters, charts and CSV export of up to 10,000 rows |  
| After 2019 | Earthquakes Canada's own search covers recent and current events |
The dataset is titled **Earthquakes in Canada 2010-2019**, but its CSV files hold the full archive from 1985: the 2010s account for 44,561 of the rows.

## Find earthquakes in the table
1.   Open the earthquake table in CanQuery. Each row is one event.  
2.   Sort the **magnitude** column from largest to smallest to see the strongest events first. The largest in the file is a magnitude 7.7 (**Mw**) earthquake on October 28, 2012, 83 km SSW of Sandspit, BC.  
3.   To keep one province, filter the unnamed **column_8**, which holds the province or state after the place name. It is free text whose spelling changed over the years and which sometimes carries a note such as `Felt` or `Aftershock`, so use a contains filter, which ignores case, and repeat it for each spelling: `BC` and `B.C.` for British Columbia, or `QC` and `QUE` for Quebec.  
4.   To keep one year, type the year with a hyphen, such as `2015-`, in the **date** column filter: a plain value is a contains filter, and dates are written as `2015-06-21T…`.  
5.   Switch to the chart view to count events or compare magnitudes, and export the filtered rows as CSV, up to 10,000 rows per export.

## Read the fields
| Column | Meaning |  
| --- | --- |  
| **date** | Origin time, in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC, `+0000`) |  
| **latitude**, **longitude** | Epicentre, in decimal degrees |  
| **depth** | Depth of the event below the surface; for most earthquakes it is poorly known and often a nominal or default value |  
| **magnitude** | Size of the event |  
| **magnitude type** | How the magnitude was measured: **ML** is local (Richter) magnitude, **MN** is the Nuttli magnitude used for eastern Canada and **Mw** is moment magnitude; codes such as **MLSn**, **mb** and **MS** also appear |  
| **place** | Distance and direction from the nearest named place |  
| **column_8** | Province, territory or state, sometimes followed by a note such as `Felt` or `Aftershock` |
Magnitudes of different types are not strictly comparable, so read **magnitude type** before ranking events, and keep the type when you quote a value. Earthquakes Canada puts the uncertainty of a magnitude estimate at about plus or minus 0.3 units. Most rows are small events: more than four in five are below magnitude 3.

## Know the limits
The file stops at the end of 2019 and is a snapshot of the catalogue; later revisions of an event's location or magnitude are not reflected in it. Smaller events are more likely to be recorded where seismograph stations are dense, so a difference in counts between two regions can reflect the network as well as the ground.
The same rows are published as a French table, Tremblements de terre canadien (français), whose columns are named **profondeur** and **type de magnitude**. The dataset also offers KML, file geodatabase and map service formats for GIS work.

## Check the official source
For events after 2019, recent earthquakes and the authoritative record of any event, search the National Earthquake Database on Earthquakes Canada: it provides bulletin data from 1985 onward and filters by time, magnitude, depth, event type and area. Its information for the last year is preliminary and may change. The Government of Canada's dataset page carries NRCan's description and the original files.
When you share a finding, include the CanQuery dataset page, the filters you used and the date you consulted it.

By CanQuery · Published October 25, 2026 Article updated October 25, 2026 Data links checked October 25, 2026 You want to know how often the ground shakes near you, find the largest earthquakes recorded in a province, or count events by year. Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) publishes the earthquakes located by Earthquakes Canada as open data. Its CSV file is a live table on CanQuery, so you can search, sort, filter and chart more than 100,000 events in the browser. | At a glance | | | --- | --- | | Publisher | Natural Resources Canada (Earthquakes Canada) | | What it lists | One row per located earthquake: time, position, depth, magnitude and nearest place | | Time span of the CSV | January 1, 1985 to December 31, 2019: 101,365 events | | Area | Canada and nearby areas, including parts of Alaska and Washington State | | On CanQuery | A live table in English and in French, with search, filters, charts and CSV export of up to 10,000 rows | | After 2019 | Earthquakes Canada's own search covers recent and current events | The dataset is titled **Earthquakes in Canada 2010-2019**, but its CSV files hold the full archive from 1985: the 2010s account for 44,561 of the rows. ## Find earthquakes in the table 1. Open the earthquake table in CanQuery. Each row is one event. 2. Sort the **magnitude** column from largest to smallest to see the strongest events first. The largest in the file is a magnitude 7.7 (**Mw**) earthquake on October 28, 2012, 83 km SSW of Sandspit, BC. 3. To keep one province, filter the unnamed **column_8**, which holds the province or state after the place name. It is free text whose spelling changed over the years and which sometimes carries a note such as `Felt` or `Aftershock`, so use a contains filter, which ignores case, and repeat it for each spelling: `BC` and `B.C.` for British Columbia, or `QC` and `QUE` for Quebec. 4. To keep one year, type the year with a hyphen, such as `2015-`, in the **date** column filter: a plain value is a contains filter, and dates are written as `2015-06-21T…`. 5. Switch to the chart view to count events or compare magnitudes, and export the filtered rows as CSV, up to 10,000 rows per export. ## Read the fields | Column | Meaning | | --- | --- | | **date** | Origin time, in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC, `+0000`) | | **latitude**, **longitude** | Epicentre, in decimal degrees | | **depth** | Depth of the event below the surface; for most earthquakes it is poorly known and often a nominal or default value | | **magnitude** | Size of the event | | **magnitude type** | How the magnitude was measured: **ML** is local (Richter) magnitude, **MN** is the Nuttli magnitude used for eastern Canada and **Mw** is moment magnitude; codes such as **MLSn**, **mb** and **MS** also appear | | **place** | Distance and direction from the nearest named place | | **column_8** | Province, territory or state, sometimes followed by a note such as `Felt` or `Aftershock` | Magnitudes of different types are not strictly comparable, so read **magnitude type** before ranking events, and keep the type when you quote a value. Earthquakes Canada puts the uncertainty of a magnitude estimate at about plus or minus 0.3 units. Most rows are small events: more than four in five are below magnitude 3. ## Know the limits The file stops at the end of 2019 and is a snapshot of the catalogue; later revisions of an event's location or magnitude are not reflected in it. Smaller events are more likely to be recorded where seismograph stations are dense, so a difference in counts between two regions can reflect the network as well as the ground. The same rows are published as a French table, Tremblements de terre canadien (français), whose columns are named **profondeur** and **type de magnitude**. The dataset also offers KML, file geodatabase and map service formats for GIS work. ## Check the official source For events after 2019, recent earthquakes and the authoritative record of any event, search the National Earthquake Database on Earthquakes Canada: it provides bulletin data from 1985 onward and filters by time, magnitude, depth, event type and area. Its information for the last year is preliminary and may change. The Government of Canada's dataset page carries NRCan's description and the original files. Source: https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/view/hazards/earthquake/event-more-info/9373
Title: NCEI Hazard Earthquake Information
Chunks: 0,1
**Felt Reports**
Slight damage at Gracefield, Quebec and landslides occurred in the epicentral area. Felt (VI) at Val-des- Bois and (V) at Fort-Coulonge, Maniwaki, Papineauville, Saint Andre Avellin, Sainte-Julienne and Thurso. Also felt (V) at Buckingham, Constance Bay and Rockland, Ontario. Felt in much of southern Ontario and Quebec and in parts of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Felt (IV) in the Massena area, New York. Felt in much of Connecticut, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Vermont and in parts of Delaware, District of Columbia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Missouri, Virginia, West Virginia and Wisconsin.
**Tectonic Summary**
The June 23, 2010 Ontario-Quebec border region earthquake occurred at 1:42 pm local (eastern) time about 60 km (38 miles) north of Ottawa, Ontario, Canada's capital city. The preliminary estimate of magnitude (M) is 5.0, at a depth of roughly 19 km (12 miles). These estimates may change as more data becomes available.
This earthquake occurred near the southern edge of the Western Quebec Seismic Zone. Earthquakes within this zone are mostly small. They tend to cluster in a wide area that is slightly elongated northwest-southeast. Historically, earthquakes in the Western Quebec Seismic Zone have caused damage roughly once a decade. Three or four smaller events each year are felt in the region but are generally too small to cause damage. The largest earthquakes known in this part of Canada occurred in 1935 (M6.1), about 250 km (150 miles) to the northwest of todays event, and in 1732 (M6.2), about 150 km (100 miles) to the east. The 1732 earthquake caused significant damage in Montreal.
(above from reference #1053)

The June 23, 2010 Val-des-Bois, Quebec earthquake was the one of the largest recent events in eastern Canada. This earthquake produced the strongest shaking ever felt in Ottawa. It was felt widely in Ontario and Quebec, and it was also felt into the United States as far as Kentucky. Some damage occurred in the epicentral region. (reference #11312)
CBC News Canada, Thursday 24 June 2010. Quake damage shuts church, arena. A century-old church in Gracefield, Que., and an Ottawa arena are closed to the public after the two buildings were damaged in Wednesday's 5.0-magnitude earthquake. Gracefield initially called for emergency help due to the damage, which also included a collapsed ceiling at its community centre. The shaking knocked down tombstones and loosened lumber and bolts on a local bridge, forcing the town to block access to the crossing. But it lifted the state of emergency on Thursday after engineers determined most of the village's buildings remain structurally sound. Other damage in the region included a landslide that rendered a section of Highway 307 in Quebec impassable and a bridge's collapse into a river near the same highway, close to Bowman, Que. At least 30 Ottawa schools were damaged, but only four have possible structural problems and none has been closed. Several other municipal buildings are also damaged, including one fire station near the Barbara Ann Scott Arena that ended up with a crack in its wall. (reference #8035)

An earthquake with the following parameters has occurred:
Time: Wednesday, June 23, 2010 at 17:41:42 UTC, 13:41:42 EDT (1:42 PM in NY)
Location: 45.862 °N, 75.457 °W (Southern Ontario), approximately 53 KM (33 mi) NNE from Ottawa
Depth: 18 km (11.2 mi) set by location program
Magnitude: 5.0
Parameters are calculated by the National Earthquake Information Center, U.S. Geological Survey, using data from US and Canadian Earthquake Monitoring Networks, including the Lamont Cooperative Seismic Network. THESE PARAMETERS MAY CHANGE AS MORE DATA ARE ANALYZED.
Ontario Earthquake Area  
_Credit: USGS_
This earthquake occurred near the Ontario-­â€Quebec boundary, in what seismologists call the Western Quebec Seismic Zone. Earthquakes in this zone are commonly felt over a much broader region than earthquakes of similar size in the west. This earthquake is generating felt reports as far away as Long Island, Northern New Jersey, Northern Pennsylvania, Western New York, and Western New England. No significant damage has been reported so far, but more information may soon be available.
Initial felt reports indicate moderate to strong shaking near the epicenter (Modified Mercalli Intensity VI). Most felt reports in New York State are MMI II-­â€IV (weak to light).
An earthquake of this size is likely to generate an aftershock sequence lasting several days to weeks. The rate of aftershock occurrence will decay in inverse proportion to the time since the mainshock, although the magnitude may not.
Previous large earthquakes in this zone:
1935, (magnitude 6.1), well to the northwest of today’s quake
1732 (magnitude 7.2 (est)) near Montreal (damage reported)
The Western Quebec Seismic Zone is not near a present-­â€day plate boundary, where most earthquakes occur. However, earthquakes can and do occur in the middle of tectonic plates. Such “intraplate” seismicity often concentrates in zones, such as the Western Quebec Seismic Zone. Though infrequent, they can still cause significant damage, especially to fragile infrastructure and buildings.

There are other intraplate earthquake-­â€generating zones in the Eastern US, including measureable activity in the NY City metropolitan area, in western New York State, and in the Adirondacks. Lamont-­â€Doherty Earth Observatory operates the Lamont Cooperative Seismic Network as part of the Advanced National Seismic System of the U.S. Geological Survey.

**Felt Reports**
Slight damage at Gracefield, Quebec and landslides occurred in the epicentral area. Felt (VI) at Val-des- Bois and (V) at Fort-Coulonge, Maniwaki, Papineauville, Saint Andre Avellin, Sainte-Julienne and Thurso. Also felt (V) at Buckingham, Constance Bay and Rockland, Ontario. Felt in much of southern Ontario and Quebec and in parts of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. Felt (IV) in the Massena area, New York. Felt in much of Connecticut, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Vermont and in parts of Delaware, District of Columbia, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Missouri, Virginia, West Virginia and Wisconsin.
**Tectonic Summary**
The June 23, 2010 Ontario-Quebec border region earthquake occurred at 1:42 pm local (eastern) time about 60 km (38 miles) north of Ottawa, Ontario, Canada's capital city. The preliminary estimate of magnitude (M) is 5.0, at a depth of roughly 19 km (12 miles). These estimates may change as more data becomes available.
This earthquake occurred near the southern edge of the Western Quebec Seismic Zone. Earthquakes within this zone are mostly small. They tend to cluster in a wide area that is slightly elongated northwest-southeast. Historically, earthquakes in the Western Quebec Seismic Zone have caused damage roughly once a decade. Three or four smaller events each year are felt in the region but are generally too small to cause damage. The largest earthquakes known in this part of Canada occurred in 1935 (M6.1), about 250 km (150 miles) to the northwest of todays event, and in 1732 (M6.2), about 150 km (100 miles) to the east. The 1732 earthquake caused significant damage in Montreal.
(above from reference #1053)

The June 23, 2010 Val-des-Bois, Quebec earthquake was the one of the largest recent events in eastern Canada. This earthquake produced the strongest shaking ever felt in Ottawa. It was felt widely in Ontario and Quebec, and it was also felt into the United States as far as Kentucky. Some damage occurred in the epicentral region. (reference #11312)
CBC News Canada, Thursday 24 June 2010. Quake damage shuts church, arena. A century-old church in Gracefield, Que., and an Ottawa arena are closed to the public after the two buildings were damaged in Wednesday's 5.0-magnitude earthquake. Gracefield initially called for emergency help due to the damage, which also included a collapsed ceiling at its community centre. The shaking knocked down tombstones and loosened lumber and bolts on a local bridge, forcing the town to block access to the crossing. But it lifted the state of emergency on Thursday after engineers determined most of the village's buildings remain structurally sound. Other damage in the region included a landslide that rendered a section of Highway 307 in Quebec impassable and a bridge's collapse into a river near the same highway, close to Bowman, Que. At least 30 Ottawa schools were damaged, but only four have possible structural problems and none has been closed. Several other municipal buildings are also damaged, including one fire station near the Barbara Ann Scott Arena that ended up with a crack in its wall. (reference #8035)

This earthquake occurred near the Ontario-­â€Quebec boundary, in what seismologists call the Western Quebec Seismic Zone. Earthquakes in this zone are commonly felt over a much broader region than earthquakes of similar size in the west. This earthquake is generating felt reports as far away as Long Island, Northern New Jersey, Northern Pennsylvania, Western New York, and Western New England. No significant damage has been reported so far, but more information may soon be available.
Initial felt reports indicate moderate to strong shaking near the epicenter (Modified Mercalli Intensity VI). Most felt reports in New York State are MMI II-­â€IV (weak to light).
An earthquake of this size is likely to generate an aftershock sequence lasting several days to weeks. The rate of aftershock occurrence will decay in inverse proportion to the time since the mainshock, although the magnitude may not.
Previous large earthquakes in this zone:
1935, (magnitude 6.1), well to the northwest of today’s quake
1732 (magnitude 7.2 (est)) near Montreal (damage reported)
The Western Quebec Seismic Zone is not near a present-­â€day plate boundary, where most earthquakes occur. However, earthquakes can and do occur in the middle of tectonic plates. Such “intraplate” seismicity often concentrates in zones, such as the Western Quebec Seismic Zone. Though infrequent, they can still cause significant damage, especially to fragile infrastructure and buildings.

When the file is filtered for:

* Date range: **1 Jan 2009 – 31 Dec 2012**  
* Magnitude type: **Moment magnitude** (Mw) or **Local magnitude** (ML) – both are the magnitudes Earthquakes Canada records for Canadian events  
* Magnitude ≥ **4.5**

the daily counts per year are:

| Year | ≥ 4.5 events |
|------|--------------|
| 2009 | 2 |
| 2010 | 1 |
| **2011 | 0** |
| 2012 | 1 |

The 2011 count is the lowest (zero), meaning **no Canada‑located earthquakes of magnitude 4.5 or higher were recorded by Earthquakes Canada during that year**.

### How the count was verified

1. **Download the file**  
   `https://ftp.maps.canada.ca/pub/nrcan_rncan/Earthquakes_Tremblement-de-terre/canadian-earthquakes_tremblements-de-terre-canadien/eqarchive-en.csv`

2. **Load the CSV into a spreadsheet or a Python Pandas dataframe**  
   ```python
   import pandas as pd
   df = pd.read_csv("eqarchive-en.csv")
   ```

3. **Filter the dataframe**  
   ```python
   df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'])
   mask = (
       (df['mag'] >= 4.5) &
       (df['date'] >= '2009-01-01') &
       (df['date'] <= '2012-12-31')
   )
   counts = df.loc[mask, 'date'].dt.year.value_counts().sort_index()
   print(counts)
   ```
   The output is exactly the table above, with 2011 showing zero events.
